opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it started from frustration more than any grand plan. When I was an undergrad at Tsinghua, I was running a lot of RL experiments, and I tried the existing libraries, RLlib among them. RLlib is very powerful, but it's built for large-scale distributed training, so it carries a lot of abstraction. When I wanted to change one small thing in an algorithm, I had to dig through layer after layer of code just to find where the logic lived. For a student doing research, that overhead really hurt.

What I wanted was something small and transparent. You should be able to read the whole codebase in an afternoon, understand exactly what each line does, and modify an algorithm without fighting the framework. Research is about trying weird ideas quickly, and the library should get out of your way.

Speed was also a factor. A lot of RL code back then was surprisingly slow for simple single-machine experiments, mostly because of how data collection and the replay buffer were handled. I thought that if I designed the core pieces carefully, like a unified buffer, a collector that works across environments, and a clean policy interface, I could make it both modular and fast.

There was also a personal side to it. Building something from scratch is the best way to really understand it. Writing Tianshou forced me to understand every detail of these algorithms, which I wouldn't have gotten by patching someone else's system. So I'd say it was about simplicity, speed, and learning, and I was a bit stubborn too.

r001.rationale: The candidate says RLlib’s layers of abstraction made it hard to locate algorithm logic and change even a small thing, creating overhead for his research experiments.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it came down to what I actually needed day to day. RLlib is a serious piece of engineering, but it's built around Ray, and that brings a whole distributed systems stack with it. Back when I started, I was a student running experiments on a few machines, and most of the time I just wanted to tweak an algorithm, run it on Atari or MuJoCo, and see the curve. With RLlib I'd be fighting the abstractions. If you wanted to change something small in how the policy updated, you'd end up touching config dictionaries, trainer classes, worker setups, and it was hard to see where your change actually landed.

So the motivation for Tianshou was really about having a clean, readable core. I wanted every algorithm to be a single, fairly short file that someone could open and understand in one sitting, with a shared set of building blocks like the collector, the replay buffer, and the policy interface. The idea was that you could write a new algorithm by composing those pieces instead of inheriting from five layers of framework code.

Another thing was performance for the single machine case. I spent a lot of effort on vectorized environments and on making the buffer and data flow efficient, because that's where most research time was going. A lot of frameworks were designed first for scaling out across a cluster, and then the small-scale case became an afterthought.

And I'll admit there was a pedagogical side to it. I learned RL by reimplementing algorithms, and I thought a library whose code you could read as a textbook would be useful for other people in that position. RLlib is great if your problem is really scaling, but if your problem is understanding and iterating, I think a simpler codebase is the right tool.

r001.rationale: The candidate says RLlib’s abstractions made small policy-update changes difficult, requiring work across config dictionaries, trainer classes, and worker setups.

astra-6.text:
For me, the main reason was flexibility. When you’re doing reinforcement learning research, you need to understand what the code is doing and be able to change it easily. Adapting a larger framework like RLlib can mean spending a lot of time understanding its abstractions before you can test your own idea.

With Tianshou, I wanted a lightweight, modular design where I could reuse the common pieces but still control the algorithm and training process. Building from scratch gave me that freedom. The goal wasn’t to recreate everything RLlib offered; it was to make experimentation easier.

r001.rationale: The response says RLlib’s abstractions could take substantial time to understand before testing an idea, making it harder to change the code for research experiments.

sol-6.1.text:
I wanted something lightweight that I could understand and change easily. In reinforcement learning research, you often need to modify the training loop, the data collection, or the algorithm itself. With a larger framework like RLlib, adapting those pieces can mean first learning a lot of infrastructure.

So the motivation for Tianshou was to keep those components clear and modular: policies, data collection, replay buffers, and training. Building from scratch gave us control over those interfaces and made it easier to experiment without bringing in complexity we didn’t need.

r001.rationale: The response says that adapting RLlib’s training, data collection, or algorithm components could require learning substantial infrastructure, motivating a simpler, modular framework for easier experimentation.
